newsitem.title: USA: Florida Gas Utility plans first bond issue.
newsitem.headline: Florida Gas Utility plans first bond issue.

text.p: Florida Gas Utility plans its first bond issue for mid-November and will use the proceeds to prepay for natural gas supplies, Finance Director Nancy Holloway said Friday.
"Issue size is still somewhat in the air," Holloway said. "It could probably range anywhere down as low as $120 million up to $250 million."
Bear Stearns & Co Inc is senior manager on the deal with co-managers Merrill Lynch & Co, PaineWebber Inc, Citicorp Securities Inc and William R. Hough & Co.

As a first-time issuer, the utility must undergo bond validation in court. A hearing is set for Oct 10, and the bonds will be issued soon after the 30-day validation appeal period ends, Holloway said.
The municipal joint action agency is headquartered in Gainesville and began operation in 1990. It manages natural gas requirements for 16 member cities.

Members include small local distribution systems such as that in the Florida Panhandle town of Jay, to larger combined electrical generating and gas distribution systems such as Gainesville Regional Utilities.

"Fourteen of our 16 members are signed up as participants in the transaction. We also have received letters of intent from two cities not currently members -- Lakeland and Orlando Utilities Commissions," Holloway said.
The bonds will be issued as Florida Gas Utility debt, secured by contracts with the participants. Debt service will be paid according to participation share.
The bonds will probably be insured and will be issued as serials with maturities up to 10 years. Call provisions have not yet been set.
The utility has had informal discussions with rating agencies but has not yet sought a rating, Holloway said.
Bond proceeds will be used to prepay for natural gas, enabling the utility to lock in prices for about one-fourth of the supply its members will need over the next 10 years.
Municipal Gas Authority of Georgia has done similar deals, although "There haven't been that many of these types of transactions actually done," Holloway said.
